why: Irrelevant context doesn't just cost tokens, it dilutes the signal — the model has to work harder to figure out what's actually relevant, which increases the odds it focuses on the wrong thing.

title: Show the model an example of the output you want
description: One concrete example of the desired format or style (few-shot) often steers output more reliably than a paragraph of abstract instructions.
why: A model imitating a concrete example has less room to misinterpret your description of "concise" or "formal" than one trying to infer those qualities from adjectives alone.

title: State constraints explicitly, don't assume defaults
description: Say what should NOT change, which files are off-limits, or what approach to avoid — the model can't infer a boundary you never mentioned.
why: The model optimizes for a plausible answer to the literal prompt — anything you leave unsaid is fair game, so an unstated constraint gets violated as often as it gets guessed correctly.

title: Break large tasks into smaller steps
description: Ask for one well-defined step at a time, or use a planning step first, rather than one giant prompt covering an entire multi-part task.
why: A model reasoning over a large, multi-part task in one pass is more likely to drop a requirement — smaller steps are individually easier to get right and to verify.

title: Iterate instead of writing the perfect prompt upfront
description: Treat the first response as a draft — refine with follow-up corrections rather than trying to anticipate every requirement in one exhaustive initial prompt.
why: It's often faster to correct a close answer than to predict every edge case in advance, and the model's own draft frequently reveals ambiguities you hadn't thought to specify.

title: Tell the model what "done" looks like
description: Define acceptance criteria — tests passing, a specific output format, a behavior to verify — instead of leaving success open to interpretation.
why: Without a concrete definition of done, neither you nor the model has an objective way to tell whether the output actually satisfies the request or just looks plausible.

title: Separate instructions from the data they operate on
description: Clearly delineate the actual task instructions from any pasted content (code, logs, documents) the model should read or transform.
why: A model can't reliably tell where your instruction ends and pasted content begins unless you mark the boundary — that ambiguity is also how prompt injection from untrusted content sneaks in.

title: Ask the model to explain its reasoning for non-trivial decisions
description: For a design choice or debugging conclusion, ask for the reasoning behind it, not just the final answer.
why: A plausible-sounding answer with no visible reasoning is harder to verify — seeing the reasoning lets you catch a flawed assumption before you act on a wrong conclusion.

title: Correct mistakes directly instead of restarting the conversation
description: Point out specifically what was wrong and why, in the same conversation, rather than abandoning it and starting a fresh prompt from scratch.
why: A fresh prompt throws away the context the model already built up about your actual intent — a direct correction lets it fix just the wrong part while keeping everything it got right.

title: Use system/role instructions for standing preferences
description: Put durable preferences — coding style, tone, constraints that apply to every request — in a persistent instruction file instead of repeating them each time.
why: Repeating the same preferences in every prompt wastes tokens and is easy to forget — a standing instruction applies automatically without you having to remember to restate it.

title: Match your prompt's detail to the task's ambiguity
description: A well-defined, narrow task needs less scaffolding than an open-ended or judgment-heavy one — don't over-specify the trivial and under-specify the ambiguous.
why: Over-specifying a simple task wastes effort on ceremony that doesn't change the outcome, while under-specifying a genuinely ambiguous one leaves the actual risk unaddressed.

title: Trim conversation history instead of letting it grow unbounded
description: Summarize or clear stale context — resolved subtasks, superseded file contents — instead of carrying a long session's full history forward indefinitely.
why: Every prior message the model re-reads costs tokens on every subsequent turn, and irrelevant history dilutes the model's attention on what's actually still relevant.

title: Reference files instead of pasting their full contents
description: When the model can read a file itself through a tool, point it at the file path rather than pasting the entire contents into the prompt.
why: Pasted content is duplicated into every subsequent turn of the conversation, while a file reference the model reads on demand is paid for once, not repeatedly.

title: Ask for a diff or targeted change, not a full file rewrite
description: When editing existing code, ask for the specific change rather than having the model reproduce the entire file in its response.
why: Reproducing an unchanged 500-line file to alter three lines spends nearly all its output tokens restating what already exists — the useful signal is a tiny fraction of the response.

title: Cache and reuse stable context across requests
description: Where the platform supports prompt caching, structure prompts so stable content — system instructions, unchanging reference material — comes first and stays identical across calls.
why: A cache hit on unchanged content skips reprocessing it entirely — a prompt where the same prefix repeats verbatim turns repeated full-price reads into cheap cache hits.

title: Scope tool output to what's actually needed
description: Request a specific line range, a filtered search, or a summary instead of dumping an entire large file or unfiltered command output into context.
why: An unfiltered search result or a whole large file consumes context budget with mostly-irrelevant content, crowding out room for the parts that actually matter to the task.

title: Avoid asking the model to repeat information it already produced
description: Refer back to an earlier answer — "use the function you just wrote" — instead of asking the model to restate it in full before continuing.
why: Regenerating already-produced content is pure overhead — it adds no new information and just spends tokens reproducing what's already sitting in the conversation.

title: Choose the smallest capable model for routine subtasks
description: Route simple, well-defined subtasks — formatting, extraction, classification — to a smaller/cheaper model and reserve a larger one for genuinely hard reasoning.
why: A task a small model handles reliably doesn't get better results from a larger one — it just costs more per token for the same outcome.

title: Close out finished subtasks instead of keeping them live
description: Once a subtask is verified complete, let it drop out of active context — via summarization or a new session — rather than keeping its full exploration history live.
why: Exploration that led to a dead end or a now-resolved question still costs tokens on every future turn if it stays in context, even though its useful conclusion could be captured in one line.

title: Verify AI output before relying on it
description: Treat a model's answer as a draft to check, especially for facts, citations, or security-sensitive code — not as ground truth by default.
why: A model can produce a fluent, confident-sounding answer that's factually wrong with no visible signal distinguishing it from a correct one — verification is the only reliable defense.

title: Keep a human in the loop for high-stakes or irreversible actions
description: Require explicit review and approval before an AI-driven action that's destructive, hard to reverse, or affects shared systems — deployments, deletions, financial transactions.
why: An AI agent can act confidently on a flawed premise just as easily as a correct one, and for irreversible actions there's no way to undo the consequence of it being wrong.

title: Give the model tools instead of asking it to simulate them
description: Where accuracy matters — a calculation, a live lookup, running actual code — connect the model to a real tool rather than relying on it to produce the answer from memory or estimation.
why: A model asked to compute or recall something a tool could do exactly is prone to a plausible-looking but wrong answer — a real tool call replaces that guess with an actual, checkable result.

title: Don't treat model confidence as a proxy for correctness
description: A firmly-stated answer isn't more likely to be right than a hedged one — the model's tone doesn't track its actual certainty the way a human expert's does.
why: Models are trained to produce fluent, assertive text regardless of whether the underlying claim is well-supported, so confident phrasing carries much less evidential weight than it does from a person.

title: Match the task to what the model is actually good at
description: Lean on AI for drafting, summarizing, exploring options, and pattern-matching across large context — and lean less on it for tasks needing guaranteed precision or novel judgment with no precedent.
why: A model's strength is statistical pattern completion over what it's seen before — tasks that fit that shape go well, and tasks requiring guaranteed exactness or genuinely novel judgment are where it's most likely to confidently miss.

title: Review AI-generated code as carefully as human-written code
description: Apply the same review standards — security, edge cases, test coverage — to AI-authored changes as to a human contributor's PR, not a lighter pass because it "looks clean".
why: AI-generated code can look idiomatic and well-formatted while still containing a logic error or security gap — fluency in style is not the same signal as correctness.

title: Be explicit about what the AI should NOT do
description: For an agent with access to real systems, state boundaries — files it shouldn't touch, actions that need confirmation — rather than assuming it will infer them from good judgment alone.
why: A model without an explicit boundary acts on the literal scope of the request, which can be broader than what you actually intended it to touch.

title: Build feedback into your AI workflow, not just the final output
description: Correct the model's intermediate assumptions or plan before it executes on them, rather than only reviewing the finished result.
why: Catching a wrong assumption at the planning stage costs one correction — catching the same wrong assumption after a full implementation is built on top of it costs redoing the implementation too.

title: Understand the limits of the model's knowledge cutoff
description: For anything that depends on recent events, current versions, or live data, have the model verify against a live source rather than relying on training data with a cutoff date.
why: A model answering from memory about anything after its training cutoff is extrapolating, not recalling — it can produce a fluent answer about a library version or event it was never actually trained on.

title: Treat AI as a collaborator to direct, not an oracle to defer to
description: Bring your own judgment to an AI's suggestion — push back, ask for alternatives, and make the final call yourself rather than accepting the first answer because it sounds authoritative.
why: The model doesn't have your full context, stakes, or accountability for the outcome — deferring to it as an oracle transfers a decision to something with less information about the situation than you have.

title: Build one immutable artifact and promote it through every environment
description: Build the container image (or package) exactly once per commit, tag it with the commit SHA, and deploy that same artifact to staging and then production — never rebuild from source for each environment.
why: Rebuilding per environment means what passed testing in staging isn't provably what's running in prod — a different dependency resolution, base image patch, or build-time environment variable could produce a subtly different artifact. Promoting the identical, already-scanned and already-tested image removes that gap entirely.

title: Make automated checks a hard gate, not an advisory one
description: Configure the pipeline so a failing test, security scan, or lint step stops the deployment outright, with no manual override path in the normal flow — not a status that's merely displayed for a human to weigh.
why: A gate anyone can click past under deadline pressure isn't a gate, it's a suggestion — and the one time it gets overridden to hit a date is usually the time it mattered. Removing the override path is what actually lets deployment be automatic without a human needing to compensate for the gate's weakness.

title: Roll production changes out progressively, never all at once
description: Use a canary or blue-green strategy that exposes a new deployment to a small slice of production traffic first, and only widen to 100% after that slice looks healthy.
why: A bug that reaches 100% of traffic instantly turns a deploy into an outage; the same bug caught at 5% of traffic is a contained incident affecting a fraction of users for a much shorter window, and gives automation time to catch it before it spreads further.

title: Trigger rollback from metrics automatically, don't wait for a human to notice
description: Wire the deployment pipeline to watch error rate, latency, and saturation during a rollout and automatically revert to the previous artifact the moment a defined threshold is breached.
why: The gap between "a bad deploy going out" and "someone noticing the dashboard" is where most of the damage from a bad deploy actually happens. A metrics-triggered auto-rollback closes that gap to roughly the length of one monitoring interval instead of however long it takes a human to be looking at the right graph.

title: Scan the built artifact for vulnerabilities before it is allowed to deploy
description: Run a dependency and container-image vulnerability scan (e.g. Trivy, Snyk) against the exact artifact that will ship, as a blocking pipeline stage, in addition to scanning source code with SAST.
why: A source-code scan alone misses vulnerabilities introduced by the base image or a transitive dependency pulled in only at build time — scanning the final artifact catches the actual thing about to run in production, not just the code that produced it.

title: Run automated smoke tests immediately after every deployment
description: After a new version reaches an environment (staging or a production canary), automatically hit its critical paths (login, checkout, the top few endpoints) and fail the pipeline if they don't respond correctly, before traffic is widened further.
why: Pre-deploy tests run against a build; smoke tests run against the actual deployed instance with its real configuration, network policies, and secrets wired up — catching an entire class of "worked in CI, broken in the real environment" failures that no amount of pre-deploy testing can see.

title: Separate "deployed" from "released" using feature flags for risky changes
description: Ship a risky change to production behind a feature flag that defaults off, and enable it for real users as a separate, instantly reversible step from the deployment itself.
why: Continuous deployment means code reaches prod constantly, which is only safe if reaching prod doesn't automatically mean reaching every user — a flag lets you turn a risky feature off in seconds without a rollback (a new deployment) at all, and lets you separate 'is the code broken' from 'is the feature a bad idea' as two independently reversible decisions.
